newsitem.title: UK: Greene collection raises 220,000 pounds at auction.
newsitem.headline: Greene collection raises 220,000 pounds at auction.

text.p: A huge archive of works by late British author Graham Greene raised more than 220,000 pounds ($365,000) at an auction on Monday.
The most coveted prize was a proof of his autobiographical novel "The End of the Affair".
The collection of more than 200 lots, including first editions, handwritten letters and books from Greene's personal library, was sold by a New York property dealer, Clint Smullyan.
Smullyan was reported to have decided to sell the archive because there was no Greene memorabilia left to buy. The author died in 1991.
The sale raised less than auctioneers Sotheby's had hoped, with many lots failing to reach the estimated prices.
But a handful of items attracted enthusiastic bidding in the crowded auction room in central London.
A proof copy of the poignant "The End of the Affair" covered with annotations by the novelist Evelyn Waugh raised 18,000 pounds, double the estimate.
Greene had asked Waugh, a fellow Roman Catholic, to read the novel before he published it because he feared it could be too shocking.
Set in London in 1939, the novel describes a love affair based closely on Greene's own with Catherine Walston. He also sent a draft of the book to Walston.
Waugh told Greene that he would passionately defend the work, describing it as "an apostolic mission in danger of being neglected by people who were shocked by the sexuality of some of your themes".
The novel's preoccupations ran through many of Greene's works and reflected his own life and troubles.

Deeply religious -- Greene was converted to Catholicism as a young man -- he nevertheless had two affairs outside his marriage. His works reflect a lifelong struggle between what he saw as the forces of good and evil.
A series of letters to the Indian author R.K. Narayan was another popular item, raising 20,000 pounds.

Greene made Narayan his protege after a mutual friend gave him a copy of one of the budding Indian writer's novels in the 1930s. The British author found Narayan publishers and encouraged him to keep writing, despite poor sales.
"Remember a public of 500 means 10,000 readers -- library copies are supposed to average 20 copies (correct) apiece," he said in one consoling letter.
Greene's script for the classic film of his book "The Third Man", starring Orson Welles, raised 4,700 pounds, well above Sotheby's 2,500-3,000-pound estimate. ($1=.6027 Pound)
